::: {.week-meta}

## By the end of this week you can

- Estimate latent mean differences in Amos.
- Interpret a latent mean difference.
- Explain why latent and observed mean differences can disagree.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. What does partial scalar invariance allow you to do?
2. Why can FIML be no better than listwise deletion? (Week 9)

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. Compare latent means, provided enough intercepts are invariant (at least two per factor).
2. When the variables that explain why data are missing are not in the model, FIML has no information to correct with.

</details>

## This week in brief

With (partial) scalar invariance in place, you can compare latent means. This needs a mean structure: intercepts for the items and means for the factors, with one group's latent means fixed to zero as the reference.

## In the session

- Identifying latent means in Amos.
- Interpreting a latent mean difference, and comparing it with observed scale scores.

## After the session

Read the core reading with these questions in mind:

- Why must loadings and intercepts be constrained equal before latent means can be compared (pp. 264–266)?
- How are latent means identified in Amos: which group's means are fixed, and to what (pp. 269–271)?
- How does Byrne interpret the size and direction of each latent mean difference (pp. 283–288)?

## Your task this week

1. Using your partial-invariance model from Week 13, estimate the latent mean differences between later-year and first-year students for all five factors.
2. Compare them with t tests on the observed scale scores. For which construct do the two disagree most? Use the Week 13 results and the invariance app to explain why.
3. Add a subsection on group comparisons to your results draft.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. Why must one group's latent means be fixed to zero?
2. Why can latent and observed mean differences disagree?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. Latent means have no natural origin. Fixing one group's means to zero makes the other group's means interpretable as differences.
2. A non-invariant item shifts the observed scale score for reasons unrelated to the construct. The latent comparison, with that item's intercept freed, is not affected.

</details>
